subject: Simple multi-level logistic regression with considerable data

messages.author: 387e625ac4da7528
messages.subject: Simple multi-level logistic regression with considerable data
parts:
Hi Folks,

I want to apologize for my naivety as I'm new to Stan and relatively new to Bayesian modeling.  With that said, I've been struggling with implementing the 'Matt Trick' in a simple 2-level logistic regression and cannot seem to replicate what is posted in the Q&A and manual.  Normally, I wouldn't worry too much about computation time, but I'm dealing with 1 to 3 million records in what will eventually be a more complex model structure...so I hope to tweak performance as much as possible as I work towards the final model.  I've attached data simulation code and two .stan files (one with and one without MT implemented).  Both produce accurate output, but file with MT implemented is considerably slower than without...any ideas as to what I'm doing wrong or suggestions for improvement?  Does it have anything to do with the fact that I'm performing these code adjustments on alpha rather than betas?

Thanks for the help!
Peter

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simple multi-level logistic regression with considerable data
parts:
See the Betancourt and Girolami arXiv paper.

http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906

The exec summary is that with a lot of data per group, the centered parameterization
is more efficient than the non-centered ("Matt trick") version.

It probably won't make much difference, but this

for (n in 1:N)
y_hat[n] <- alpha[groups[n]] + x[n]*beta;

would probably be more efficient as

for (n in 1:N)
y_hat[n] <- alpha[groups[n]];
y_hat <- y_hat + x * beta;

The reason is that the x * beta is more efficient for derivatives
than the repeated x[n] * beta.

For efficiency, you may also want to standardize your outcome and
predictors and tighten the priors.

You might also find that giving beta a hierarchical prior is more
efficient than the fixed normal(0, 5), especially if normal(0, 5)
isn't a good description of the fitted parameters.

- Bob

Excellent, thanks for the reply Dr. Carpenter.  I'll give the paper a read so that I better understand when and when not to use the non-centered treatment.  As far as parsing out components of y_hat estimation, this makes a lot of sense and will incorporate the change directly.  Interestingly, I standardized the real data, but didn't do so with my simulated data...too much of me trying to replicate what others have done rather than thinking about what I need to accomplish!  Appreciate your help and patience.

Cheers,
Peter
